title: It Works If We Work It
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart shares a note from a teacher named Katie, whose focus on core credibility-building habits -- MGCs (Moments of Genuine Connection), mini-sermons, using class time well, and fast feedback -- paid off when a parent reported that her son could tell she was a good, passionate teacher. Stuart uses the anecdote to make a broader point: for every compliment a teacher receives, there are dozens of equally appreciative students and parents who never say anything, so absence of feedback isn't evidence of absence of impact. He illustrates this with his own story of running into a former student, Scarlett, years later and learning that a simple classroom practice had mattered to her. The piece closes with two practical takeaways: tell people today that you see and value their work, and trust that unglamorous, fundamental practices compound in effect even when the payoff isn't visible in the moment.
points: Stuart's "silent majority" argument: for every explicit compliment a teacher gets, there are "dozens of others you won't" receive, so felt impact is a poor measure of actual impact.

Katie's win came from stacking basic, un-flashy fundamentals (MGCs, mini-sermons, time management, fast feedback) rather than any novel technique -- Stuart frames consistency as the differentiator, not novelty.
The Scarlett grocery-store anecdote functions as evidence that classroom practices can register with students in ways teachers never learn about until much later, if ever.
Two actionable takeaways close the piece: proactively thank people whose work has affected you, and keep trusting foundational practices even on days when their effect isn't visible.
quotes: Just wanted to say thank you for putting words to what I always vaguely knew to be true about teacher credibility. As I started the school year, I really focused on MGCs, mini sermons, using time well, and giving quick feedback and grades.

Whenever I hear of a teacher compliment like the one Katie received, I always remind myself: for every one that you receive, there are dozens of others you won't. Meaning, when we're blessed to receive a thank-you from a student or a compliment from a parent, we have to remember that, commonsensically, there are dozens of other folks who also appreciate our work but haven't reached out.

It's like that time I ran into Scarlett at the grocery store. Here was a student I assumed I had failed to help, yet who, years later through a chance run-in at the grocery store, was able to tell me that my seemingly simple classroom practice had made a difference in her life.
So one takeaway here is, let's tell those folks today that we see them, we value their hard work, we've experienced the fruits of their labors.
It's not a newfangled list. Nothing flashy or impressive about it. But WOW do these things ever work if we work them.
